attribution.note: Marcus's own words in the interview, published on his Substack. He is speaking for himself, not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: An unhedged statement about OpenAI's present financial position. Limiting the comparison to the rivals he named (Anthropic, Google, maybe Amazon) fits the context. It is correctly classed as an observation.

contract.note: Reading the phrase as spending stretched relative to assets, plus the largest commitments, is the fair, ordinary plain reading. Using May 2026 as the period is the evaluator's choice but a reasonable one. With no accounting basis named, the contract rules out a supported or contradicted money verdict.

evidence.note: Alphabet's own disclosure of its cash and debt at 31 March 2026. It covers one comparator only and is outside May. It says nothing about OpenAI's burn or commitments.
Anthropic's own announcement of new compute agreements on 28 May 2026. It gives no dollar obligations and no cash-burn or asset figures, so no comparison can be made from it.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched May 2026 figures on spending, assets and commitments for OpenAI and the named rivals. The two items describe only Alphabet's balance sheet and Anthropic's compute deals. Because the accounting basis is unknown, the contract also bars a money verdict. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own essay text. He cites tweets and Bloomberg for the loan news, but the forecast about the IPO is his own.

semantics.note: 'Going to be hard' is unhedged, so it counts as a scored forecast. 'Given this news' is kept as a stated reason. No deadline was given. The hedged 'maybe' and 'might' remarks that follow are correctly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'hard' as material investor resistance to a valuation above the private round is fair and ordinary. Requiring evidence that any delay is linked to valuation, and not inferring it from delay alone, is balanced. The valuation baseline differs between sources ($852B post-money vs $730B), which the contract's consistency requirement handles.

evidence.note: Bloomberg reports that the loan talks stalled and that the reason is unclear. This concerns Marcus's premise, not the IPO outcome, so it can only be context.
OpenAI's own disclosure of an $852B post-money valuation, which serves as the private-round baseline. It says nothing about IPO demand.

A secondhand report, citing the NYT and unnamed sources, that advisers offered a choice between a delay and a lower valuation. It fits Marcus's forecast but describes discussions, not a failed pricing or a decided postponement. It also gives a different baseline ($730B).
Reuters reports that OpenAI will not IPO in 2026, with Altman citing safety. That is an actual delay, but it is not shown to stem from resistance to the valuation.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and none of the evidence meets the contract's early-resolution rule. The June adviser reports suggest valuation difficulty but describe discussions only. The 2026 postponement was publicly attributed to safety, not shown to result from investor resistance. No higher-valued IPO has been completed. The forecast cannot yet be scored.
